name: Kira Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Hollis and Sons, a little family builder that does old houses: extensions, loft conversions, gutting kitchens. It's me, Ray Hollis, his son Dean and a plasterer who comes in when we need him. My day is mostly strip-outs, carrying, mixing, lifting floorboards, and lately Ray's been letting me do some of the simpler joinery, skirting and floor joists. I like that every house is different and I like that nobody sits at a computer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been with them, and what's life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years. Before that I was in a bakery packing bread, which I left because the line went automatic and they cut the night shift. I rent a one-bed flat on my own with my cat, Biscuit, and I've got about two and a half months of money saved. I don't use AI, no. I've got an old phone that does calls and messages and I like it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, fine, carry on. I wouldn't go online about it, I'm not on there much. At work I'd just say I told you so to Dean, who's always on about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to keep doing what I'm doing, which is all I want. But it doesn't mean I'm safe. Ray's sixty-three, and when he packs it in I don't know if Dean keeps the firm going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. I'd keep turning up, keep learning the joinery off Ray, and keep putting a bit by every month. If anything I'd try to get the savings up past three months before winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. Then the normal low worry comes back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you worry about at Hollis and Sons, even with AI fizzling out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My boss Ray Hollis is sixty-three, and when Ray retires I don't know if there's a job for me at all. Dean's more interested in property than building. That's my real worry and AI's got nothing to do with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anything changed already, with the firm or your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Winter's always quiet, and we lost two weeks last February. Rent went up forty a month in the summer. So the savings go down in the winter and back up in the spring, and I just try to keep them above two months.

say: I'd say **good, carry on**, and tell Dean I told him so.
I'd stay **off the internet** about it, because I'm hardly on there.
think: I'd keep doing my job, but I'm **not safe** anyway.
Ray is **sixty-three**, and nobody knows if Dean keeps the firm going.
do: Keep **learning joinery** from Ray on refurbishment jobs, a bit more each week.
Push savings past **three months** before the winter lull starts.
feel: She feels **relieved**, then the usual **low worry** returns.
S0.quote: My boss Ray Hollis is sixty-three, and when Ray retires I don't know if there's a job for me at all.
fieldNote: Her real threat is **succession** at a tiny family firm, not technology.
She has already lost a job to **automation** once, at a bakery.
Savings rise and fall with the **winter lull**, and she watches them closely.

steps.text: Keep learning skirting and joist work from Ray on refurb jobs
Push savings past three months before the winter lull

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it doesn't touch us much, because you can't send a computer up a ladder in a Victorian house. I'd probably keep my head down about it, though. People get worked up and it never helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we're further back in the queue than most. Old houses are crooked and nothing is where the drawing says. But I've seen what happened at the bakery, so I'm not daft about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and watch. If Ray brings in some app for quotes I'd leave it to Dean. I'd keep saving and maybe cut the takeaway on Fridays so the pot grows a bit faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Like hearing a storm a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the bakery going automatic. Does this remind you of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. At the bakery they said the new machines would just help us, and six months later the night shift was gone. So when people say AI just helps, I don't believe them, but I don't know what to do about it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who handles the paperwork side at Hollis and Sons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dean does it, on a laptop in his van. Quotes, ordering the timber, invoices. I suppose that's the bit that changes, and Dean would love that. It wouldn't really touch me unless it meant fewer of us were needed.

say: I'd say computers **can't climb ladders** in Victorian houses.
I'd **keep my head down** at work rather than get worked up.
think: Old crooked houses put us **further back** in the queue.
The **bakery** taught me that 'it'll just help' isn't true.
do: Leave any **quoting app** to Dean and keep working as now.
Cut the **Friday takeaway** to grow the savings faster.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, like hearing a distant storm.
S1.quote: At the bakery they said the new machines would just help us, and six months later the night shift was gone.
fieldNote: Past experience makes her **distrust promises** that machines only help.
She sees the **thinking work** at the firm, quotes and ordering, as Dean's area.
She has no plan beyond **waiting and saving**, which fits her resistant temperament.

steps.text: Leave any new quoting software to Dean and keep working
Cut the Friday takeaway to grow savings faster

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say someone needs to slow this down. I'm not one for marches, but I'd sign a petition if somebody put one in front of me. At work I'd say what everyone's saying, that we're in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means I'm out of work by the time I'm thirty-two. Two years for Dean's laptop jobs to go, then three more and robots can do strip-outs and carrying, which is most of my day. I'm the easiest one to replace on the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder straight away, no takeaways, no new clothes, nothing. I'd keep turning up and hope Ray keeps me on for the old houses. Beyond that, I honestly don't know what I'd do, and that's the worst bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. A cold feeling, like when the bakery manager called us all into the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Ray told you he was letting you go in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back to my sister's spare room, because two and a half months of rent doesn't go far without a wage. I'd look for something, but I'm not sure what's left for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Ingrid, in the first place. She's a hairdresser, so maybe her job lasts longer than mine. And the job centre, I suppose, though I've never liked going there.

say: I'd say someone in charge needs to **slow this down**.
I'd **sign a petition** if someone at work handed me one.
think: I'd be **out of work** by thirty-two, the easiest one to replace.
Robots in **2031** could do strip-outs and carrying, most of my day.
do: Stop **all spending** beyond rent and food straight away.
Keep turning up and hope Ray keeps her on for **old houses**.
Fall back on her sister **Ingrid's spare room** if the job goes.
feel: She feels **frightened**, with a cold feeling from the bakery closure.
S2.quote: I'd go back to my sister's spare room, because two and a half months of rent doesn't go far without a wage.
fieldNote: Her hands-on job gives her **three extra years**, but she can't see a use for them.
She has **no plan** beyond cutting back and hoping, and admits it.
Family, her sister **Ingrid**, is her real safety net, not the state.

steps.text: Stop buying takeaways and new clothes to protect her savings
Keep turning up and ask Ray to keep her for old houses
Move into her sister Ingrid's spare room if the job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About the same, really, a bit quieter. I'd say it's not right that it's all happening so fast. I'd keep it to friends, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means the robots come in 2034 and I'm thirty-five. I'd have more of the joinery under my belt, so maybe I'm not just the labourer. But I still think it's me who goes before Dean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ray to teach me as much joinery as he can, faster, so I'm worth more. I'd keep saving, aiming for four months. I wouldn't do anything big until I saw what was actually happening on other sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe. It's further away, but it's still coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change anything for you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to stop being the labourer and start being the one Ray trusts with a staircase. That's something. Not much, but something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever think about learning something new, given the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it was a proper trade and not computers. Like stairs, or roofing, something with your hands that robots are bad at. I'd want someone to show me it works before I jumped, though.

say: I'd say it's **not right** for change to come this fast.
I'd keep my views to **friends**, not online.
think: Robots arrive in **2034**, when I'm thirty-five, with more joinery behind me.
I still think **I go before Dean** when work shrinks.
do: Ask Ray to **teach joinery** faster, including staircases.
Wait to see **other sites** before making any big move.
S3.quote: Five years gives me time to stop being the labourer and start being the one Ray trusts with a staircase.
fieldNote: Extra time helps her mainly by moving her **up from labourer**.
She'd only retrain in a **hands-on trade** that's been shown to last.
She expects to lose out to **family loyalty** at the firm.

steps.text: Ask Ray to teach her staircases and joinery faster
Build savings toward four months of rent and bills
Watch other sites before making any bigger move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off, so let's not panic. I'd probably not talk about it much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it gives me more time to get good, which matters. But I'm still a junior, and I'll still be in the same little firm unless something changes. Ten years of waiting is still waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the first year looks the same as now. Turn up, learn from Ray, save. Maybe after a few years, if Ray retires, I'd look for another small builder doing old houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but under that a worry I can't shake. It feels far away and close at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be thirty-seven when it arrives and around forty when the robots come. How does that sit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Around forty is a terrible age to start again from nothing in a trade that robots have just walked into. I'd be too old to be an apprentice and too junior to be a boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually move, in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray retiring, probably. Or seeing a robot actually doing a strip-out with my own eyes. I'm not going to change my whole life because of a newspaper story.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long way off**, so no panic.
I'd mostly **not talk** about it at all.
think: More time lets me **get good**, but I'm still a junior.
**Ten years of waiting** is still waiting.
do: Keep turning up, **learning from Ray** and saving each month.
Look for another **old-house builder** if Ray retires.
feel: She feels uneasy on top, with a **worry she can't shake** underneath.
S4.quote: Around forty is a terrible age to start again from nothing in a trade that robots have just walked into.
fieldNote: She sees the decade as time **lost to waiting**, given her temperament.
She'd only move if she **saw a robot** or Ray retired.
Turning forty as robots arrive feels to her like a **bad age** to restart.

steps.text: Keep working and learning joinery from Ray each week
Look for another old-house builder if Ray retires

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Most of my day is carrying and stripping out, and that's exactly what a robot would do first. I've already lost one job to a machine at the bakery, and I don't want to be thirty-two and doing it again. What would help is someone paying for me to learn a proper trade, a real one, before it happens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about living alone. When it's just you, there's no second wage. If I lost this job, there's no one else's pay covering the rent.

headlineQuote: I've already lost one job to a machine at the bakery, and I don't want to be thirty-two and doing it again.
portrait: Kira is a 27-year-old **labourer** at a tiny family builder that refurbishes old houses.
She rents alone with her cat and keeps about two and a half **months saved**.
She lost a bakery job to **automation** and distrusts promises that machines only help.
She never uses AI and prefers to **wait** and see, though that frightens her in the fast scenario.
Her main fallback is her sister **Ingrid**, not the state or a new career.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when robots could take the strip-outs and carrying that fill her day.
whatWouldHelp: Someone paying for her to learn **a proper trade** before it happens.
